examples.problem_statement: If 3 ≤ x ≤ 5 and 4 ≤ y ≤ 7. Find the greatest value of xy and the least value of x/y.

solution.description: Read the endpoints off each given range, since every extreme value of an expression in x and y will come from these boundary values.
The book's rule for the product: both x and y should be highest for xy to be maximum, so take each variable at its upper endpoint.
Multiply the two chosen maxima to get the greatest value of the product xy.
The book's rule for the quotient: x should be minimum and y should be maximum for x/y to be minimum, so pair the smallest numerator with the largest denominator.

key_reminders: A product of two positive quantities is largest when both factors are at their maximum.
A quotient is smallest when the numerator is at its minimum and the denominator at its maximum.
Extremes of such expressions occur at the endpoints of the given ranges, not inside them.
common_mistakes: Using y at its minimum (4) for the least value of x/y, giving 3/4 instead of 3/7.
Mixing the two rules and pairing x_max with y_max for the quotient as well as the product.

concept.technique_name: testing cases to eliminate must-be-true statements

examples.problem_statement: If |x| > |y|, which of the following must be true? Indicate all such statements. (A) xy is positive (B) x + y > 0 (C) x^2 > y^2

solution.description: Choose a first test case and double-check it against the stem's condition, so nothing you conclude rests on values that break the given fact.
Evaluate all three statements on this first case; every one of them holds, so none can be eliminated yet.
Pick a second case that still satisfies the stem but flips the sign of x, since the absolute value signs mean x and y may be positive or negative.
Evaluate the first two statements on the sign-flipped case; the product is negative and the sum is negative, so eliminate both (A) and (B).
Check the remaining statement on the same case; it still holds, and since only one choice is left you can stop testing there.

key_reminders: A "must be true" statement is disproved by a single valid counterexample.
|x| > |y| constrains only magnitudes, so both variables may still be positive or negative.
Stop testing cases once exactly one choice survives; there is always at least one correct answer.
common_mistakes: Testing only the all-positive case x = 5, y = 3, where all three statements happen to be true.
Reading |x| > |y| as x > y and concluding x + y > 0.

concept.technique_name: area of a border as a difference of rectangles

examples.problem_statement: The figure above represents a rectangular garden with a walkway around it. The garden is 18 feet long and 12 feet wide. The walkway is uniformly 3 feet wide, and its edges meet at right angles. What is the area of the walkway?

solution.description: Find the area of the smaller rectangle, which is the garden itself, from its given length and width in square feet.
Get the length of the larger rectangle by adding twice the walkway width to the garden's length, since the walkway runs along both ends.
Get the width of the larger rectangle the same way, adding twice the walkway width to the garden's width.
Multiply those outer dimensions to find the area of the garden and walkway combined, in square feet.
Subtract the garden's area from the combined area, because the walkway is exactly the region between the two rectangles.
Confirm with the book's second approach, cutting the walkway into four 3-by-3 corner squares plus two 18-by-3 and two 12-by-3 strips.

key_reminders: A uniform border's area equals the outer rectangle's area minus the inner rectangle's area.
A border of width w adds 2w to each outer dimension, not w.
The four corner squares must be counted once when decomposing a border into pieces.
common_mistakes: Adding the walkway width only once, using 21 by 15 instead of 24 by 18.
Decomposing the walkway into four strips and double-counting or omitting the four corner squares.
Reporting the garden's area, which is also 216, without performing the subtraction that justifies it.
